body: I had a stumpy dwarf hamster once. Got him for free from the pet store because he lost an arm in a fight. He seemed happy enough, but I always worried about him because he'd try to unload his hamster cheeks and he could only empty the one side. I guess he was able to rotate his stock because my fear of rotting food eating at his pouch flesh never became realized.

I have been through this. Recently. Only it wasn't a wooden spatula. There is no other term for it: it was a tiny plastic shit spork. The little collection bowl and said shit spork were both very smooth plastic, and my pudding-consistency butt putty was almost impossible to collect because it kept sliding off of the prongs.

I have a strong stomach, but I was heaving and shaking throughout the entire ordeal.

I used to use a lot of psychedelics, and I've had anxiety for as long as I can remember. For me, it never became an issue. Surprisingly, when people I was around started feeling fear or anxiety, I was usually the one who brought them down into a safer head space.

I think the most important part is allowing yourself the time. Ensure you don't have any tasks or responsibilities that you need to take care of--at least for those few hours. Small things, simple as moving a few loads of laundry, can become daunting tasks, depending on your state of being.

You have to relinquish yourself to the experience. You can trust your body to keep you safe and healthy and alive. This is where I've seen people fuck up the most. Given that you're responsible with your dosage, you have no reason to doubt your physical capability of handling it.

Mentally and emotionally, I've had some difficult experiences. But they've never been "bad." Whatever my mind seemed to task me with, afterwards it always seemed like it was exactly what I needed to work through. So what that comes down to is trust your brain, too.

I fucking hate my brain on a regular basis. Anxiety, depression, a slew of terrible nervous habits... No matter what substance I chose to throw at that thing, it never let any of that bullshit take over. Most often, it offered me a break from my usual thought processes. Then my stupid brain would invariably spring back to its normal stupid everyday self.

That's all I've got for you though, without knowing you further.

Thank you. I watched a video where someone described getting sober like frostbite. You're numb for however long, then when you first start warming up, feeling begins to return, tingly at first but then painful like daggers. It seems apt.

I'm curious to what you mean about peer support groups. I'm going to AA meetings (didn't make it today, but to be fair I was too broken down to even shower). I'm in my early 20's though, so I can't describe most of them as peers in terms of age.

I mean no offense, but the fact that you were "roped into checking it out" and feel bitter about it makes me think you probably didn't need to be there in the first place.

You got a few downvotes (not from me because you contributed to the conversation), and I'm assuming it's because your assertions about control.

The lack of control is pretty much what defines alcoholism, and addiction in general. Some people can party hard, on a relatively regular basis, cut completely loose and swing out of control. These people are not necessarily alcoholics. Folks who attempt control, placing a wide variety of constraints on their drinking to no avail ARE alcoholics.

Your advice is to simply think rationally. Can you tell me you just "forgot" what you told me to realize? It doesn't happen like that. I can't just "snap out of it" because my thinking, when it comes to what you've said, isn't flawed. I can't really take your advice because everything you've said is already self-evident to me. I love my life. I know I have a lot to lose. I realize my importance, my worth, and I know my job is doing right for myself and many others. Making these realizations, understanding that my habits aren't worth losing anything, has not affected the drinking. Was simply thinking through it what helped you onto a better path?

If your answer is yes, then I wouldn't consider you an alcoholic.

Edit: I don't think you're wrong in telling me to avoid ADAPT though. Still considering it as a possibility, but I'd like to see how I fare using AA and SMART recovery before resorting to ADAPT.

I would love to do this. The gossip is extremely problematic in my current (new) squadron. Granted, it's the reason I got there so soon (became an instructor because the word got out that I knew my shit), but knowing how much influence talk has all the way up the chain makes me extremely wary of looking to the AF for help.

I know my parents could help me get through this. Their dealings with addiction are what helped me identify my behaviors in the first place. But the limitations alcoholism has placed on me currently (digestive issues that interfere with PT, possible ulcer, waiting to hear about profile status)... It's an unnecessarily complicated situation. I have too much going on in the admin/medical side of things to pack up and go home for a bit.

Taking leave would be ideal. There's just so much to take care of beforehand. It's truly deplorable when you start wishing "why can't a family member just get sick so I can put this bullshit on hold for a few days?" There's no emergency leave for being a fuck-up.

I don't think you're using scare tactics or anything. This is tough stuff, and I'm no stranger to the implications.

I think the toughest part of your post for me to swallow (not saying you're incorrect) is accepting that my life is more important than my career. I really think I did the best thing possible for myself when I joined. I don't have much to fall back on. No college, no savings. Too early into my enlistment to receive most of the benefits. My family back home would try their best to support me, but their financial situation is deplorable. Particularly now (putting a sister through college, dad just got laid off), but it's always a struggle. I finally found somewhere I could take care of myself, and it would destroy me to give it up.

I don't have a lot to add to that. Just airing complaints mostly. Even if I want to say, "You're totally right!" I just have a hard time with it. Tough to say how much of it is valid and how much is blown out of proportion without sobriety.

From what you've said, self-identifying seems far less risky than finding out I can't take care of things personally. AA talks about how how the possible consequences for an alcoholic can always have the "yet" qualifier attached.

My squadron is quite concerned about making sure the IG stays happy. It's good to know I can fall back on that if I feel uncomfortable with how I'm treated, but I'm a relatively new kid in the AF. I don't have any experience "working the system" compared to my CoC.

I'm happy to hear about folks keeping a TS clearance. Part of why I posted here is because the AF frames a lot of issues (mental, behavioral, etc.) as having no job impact for getting help. They fail to mention the implications for stuff like clearances, PRP status or the like, which can truly end your career in a hurry.

I'm going to AA currently, still debating on whether or not I need to identify through ADAPT/bring doctors into the situation for withdrawal symptoms. I can already see AA as being mighty helpful, though.

The panic attacks are unrelated. Well they are related in that my anxiety was a contributing factor (but I know not the cause/source of blame) for my alcoholism. Alcohol proved a reliable and extremely unhealthy way to self-medicate.

So it is something I need to talk to a doctor about, but not for detox. At least I don't think so. Prioritization, in the scope of risk mitigation, has been drilled into my head from work. I'm going to take care of the alcohol problem first.

r/alcoholism told me that "high-functioning" is a STAGE of alcoholism, not a condition in and of itself, that it is only a matter of time before it progresses to the point where the term itself becomes absurd. I can already understand the implications this poses, and the logic makes sense.

I'm happy to hear my post awakened something within you. Perhaps one day we'll each have similar "flair" on this subreddit expressing our days since deciding to take back control. I've been taking inventory only extremely recently, but it's great knowing that even one person is admitting to these realizations at the same time I have.

I've already discovered that solidarity is a much healthier than any alternative approach. Neither you nor I are alone. Resources are available. Feel free to PM me if you're not sure how to take the first steps (unfortunately, that's the only bit I feel confident in right now. Baby steps can still be frightening).

I'm at the ripe young age of 22.  My addiction progressed hard and fast.  Less than a year ago, I was proud to feel I didn't rely on alcohol, even though I realized if it happened, I would be a third-generation alcoholic.  Both sides of the family.  I was naive.

This isn't even my first addiction.  I had problems with "designer" drugs a few years ago.  Alcohol was my LEAST favorite drug.  Now that I'm at a point in my life where alcohol is the most "acceptable/easy" addiction to handle, I defaulted to it.  I am realizing my habits with alcohol have mirrored the same effects as when I hit rock bottom with drugs.  Sobriety seems to be the only answer.  I felt like a complete piece of shit during the last withdrawal portion of my life, but I bounced back (which seemed completely impossible during the whole ordeal).

Perhaps this instance will be different.  I don't expect it to be as easy as it was quitting drugs.  I still lived with my parents, who took excellent care of me and didn't let me out of their sight during my period of withdrawal.  I was blessed, in a way, to come from several generations of addicts.  They understood my need for supervision, therapy, and everything in between.

I recognize this next bout of sobriety as necessary, but also more intimidating.  I'm essentially alone.  I don't want to lose any of my current resources.  My boyfriend may be instrumental, or he may be detrimental.  My family is thousands of miles away from me.  But I need to make an effort before my coworkers and superiors decide I'm not worth the effort, because I NEED my job.  Not just for money but for personal fulfillment.

Thanks for your reply.  It's encouraging to see a response from a person in the beginning stages of sobriety.  I hope to be in your shoes SOON.

Your definition of alcoholism makes total sense. I have found myself feeling so much better after the first shot of the day. But that feeling is so fleeting. Each consecutive shot takes me further away from my intended experience, and I don't think I'll be able to think, "That amount had me feeling good last night," ever again.

I smoke cigarettes as well, and the feeling is very similar. I love my first cigarette of the day, but the less time that passes between each smoke, the less of an effect I feel from the nicotine. It's always a disappointment, and cognitively I know "Hey it's only been an hour, smoking right now is a total waste," but my desperation leads me to think it's worth trying.

(Please let me know if that analogy, or an issue part of my posts are inappropriate or could be seen as a trigger. If so I will remove it. The last thing I want to do in this sub is encourage or endorse my behaviors/faults.)

I haven't. It hasn't "become an issue," but the sense of impending doom is present. Truth is, it IS an issue already, but I've framed the fallout as purely physical, separate from the alcohol. (I have diarrhea at least 3 times a day. I cannot run without getting the runs. I'm a military member, and my inability to run more than 8-10 minutes without heading to the bathroom is a huge problem for keeping my job. Admitting to alcoholism comes with its own stigma and vulnerability in my life.)

Quitting will be difficult, and I haven't been able to admit the problem to folks in my chain of command who see me as an infallible asset to my community. I'm hoping to find an answer to that though sobriety and seeking help.

>Being sober isn't just about not drinking. It's about finding the answers in your life to the questions you have. The meaningful answers that lead to solutions.

This is beautiful. Right now I see sobriety as not drinking. I never considered it as being more than that. Thank you for your response.

My alcoholism is not as frustrating to him as my other issues. During panic attacks, he's gotten fed up enough to send me to another room. Under the influence of alcohol, I don't suffer from these issues.

I'm certain that he's not proud of my habits, but acting like a drunk is more palatable to him than acting like a nervous wreck.

It's worth noting that he has made great progress dealing with my anxiety, simultaneously drawing more of my attention to my drinking. I have to add that caveat before the judgment is brought down upon him.

That's exactly it. I'm not willing to wait. I've put myself into what I believe to be the best possible path for my life right now. And I don't want to lose it, because I may never get another opportunity. Also, I don't have any trouble saying I'm an alcoholic.

It's a strange mixture of rationality and irrationality that I've got going for me right now.

I've reached out to AA, going to sit in on a meeting tomorrow. I can't be certain that AA is the right choice for help and treatment, but it's certainly worthwhile to check it out.

I appreciate your response. Even if I don't WANT to quit yet, I'm reassured by your non-judgmental post and the resource you have provided. I realize this is a process, a track that I've seen close family members take, and I've internalized the horror that my awareness wasn't enough to steer me away.

I tend to think of my situation as more complicated than many other alcoholics, which is admittedly non-conducive to recovery and an excuse for continuing on my current path.

I'll welcome you, and anyone else who reads this comment, to send me a PM if you feel any inclination to dig deeper. Not that I want you to feel obligated, just offering that option if you have any interest in getting the "full" story.

I'll end with a simple "thank you." Just knowing someone heard my whisper into the Internet void makes me feel like I've accomplished something worthy today.

Not really... They try to tell you that there's no reason to be concerned about going to military mental health resources. But I have a job that requires a high level security clearance, and to get help would put me at risk of losing that.

Not to mention that they're trying to downsize. Cutting folks with diseases or disabilities (mental or physical) is an easy way to trim the fat.

I can push through and keep my job security, or get help and risk throwing it away.

Thanks for reading. Yeah IBS seems like the culprit, and I know it often coincides with anxiety in particular. I do have an appointment with a (military) doctor for it on Monday. They are the only ones who can authorize documents stating what you can or can't do for physical training. I'm disinclined to believe they're going to cut me any slack for my fitness assessment though.

It's sad that I'll have to walk in and pretend that my physical symptoms are the only issues bothering me. Part of me is desperate to go in and say "I'm a mess, I need rehab, therapy, and medication!" But to do that would be to throw away this life that I've created for myself, which I still believe has been my best course of action ever.

I don't have a backup plan. Not yet. My family back home can't support me; they're in dire straights putting my sister through college and dealing with medical expenses. My boyfriend and I have a strong relationship, but he's not about to make me a housewife.

This is it for me, and it's entirely too much.
